cards.explanation: The answer is the days of mourning for his father. Esau says in his heart, “The days of mourning for my father are at hand; then I will kill my brother Jacob.” (Gen 27:41) So the thing he's waiting on is the days of mourning for Isaac. I think this is a heavy one, friends, and it's okay to just sit with that. The text says Esau held a grudge because of the blessing (Gen 27:41).

The answer is her brother Laban. Rebekah tells Jacob, “…flee at once to my brother Laban in Haran.” (Gen 27:43) She sends for him, warns him about Esau's plot, and has the destination ready right then. Laban is her own brother. I think this is a tense moment, friends, and she moves fast.

The answer is fury. Rebekah says, “Stay with him for a while, until your brother’s fury subsides…” (Gen 27:44) Fury is the word she uses. Think of an oven that needs time to cool down before anyone opens the door. That's what the waiting is for.

The answer is False, and here's what the text says. Rebekah tells Jacob, “Then I will send for you and bring you back from there.” (Gen 27:45) The plan is for her to send for him. Jacob isn't left to find his own way home.

The answer is Hittite. Rebekah says, “I am weary of my life because of these Hittite women.” (Gen 27:46) Hittite is the word she uses. She goes on to ask what good her life is if Jacob takes a Hittite wife from among them. The text doesn't say more about why, so I won't guess.

The answer is True. “So Isaac called for Jacob and blessed him.” (Gen 28:1) Think about that for a second, friends. Jacob walks in after what he did in Genesis 27:35 and walks out blessed. That's the text, plain as dough.

The answer is don't marry a Canaanite woman. Isaac commands him, “Do not take a wife from the Canaanite women…” (Gen 28:1) That's the command, word for word. Then he points Jacob toward Laban's daughters (Gen 28:2). The direction comes with the rule.

The answer is Abraham. Isaac says, “And may He give the blessing of Abraham to you and your descendants…” (Gen 28:4) He's asking God Almighty to give it, as the blessing in the verse before shows (Gen 28:3). Abraham is Isaac's own father (Gen 25:19). So the blessing is the one that goes back to his dad.

The answer is the land where he lives as a foreigner. Isaac asks that God give Jacob and his descendants the blessing of Abraham, “…so that you may possess the land where you dwell as a foreigner, the land God gave to Abraham.” (Gen 28:4) That's how the blessing ends. It's the land God gave to Abraham. And Isaac is asking God for it, not handing it out himself.

The answer is Abraham's son Ishmael. The text says Esau, “…seeing that his father Isaac disapproved of the Canaanite women…” went to Ishmael and married Mahalath. (Gen 28:8-9) Mahalath is Ishmael's daughter. Ishmael is Abraham's son. So Esau goes back into the family for a wife.
The answer is False, and the text says it directly. Esau married Mahalath “…in addition to the wives he already had.” (Gen 28:9) She wasn't a replacement. She joined the wives he already had.

The answer is stones. “…taking one of the stones from that place, he put it under his head and lay down to sleep.” (Gen 28:11) A stone, friends. No fluff, no thread count, no pillow menu. That's the bedding.

The answer is a ladder. “…Jacob had a dream about a ladder that rested on the earth with its top reaching up to heaven…” (Gen 28:12) Bottom on the earth, top reaching heaven. That's what he sees while he sleeps. A very tall ladder, friends.

The answer is angels. The dream shows “…God’s angels were going up and down the ladder.” (Gen 28:12) Up AND down, friends. Jacob is lying there with a stone under his head (Gen 28:11), and the dream has angels moving on a ladder that rests on the earth and reaches to heaven.

The answer is True. The LORD says, “I will give you and your descendants the land on which you now lie.” (Gen 28:13) The land in the promise is the land under Jacob right then. He doesn't even have to get up to see the property, friends. And the promise is for his descendants too.

The answer is False, and here's what the text says. The LORD says, “All the families of the earth will be blessed through you and your offspring.” (Gen 28:14) That's all the families, not only Jacob's. The promise reaches wide, like dust spreading in every direction.

The answer is to be with him and bring him back. The LORD says, “…I am with you, and I will watch over you wherever you go, and I will bring you back to this land.” (Gen 28:15) Wherever he goes, he's not going alone. And there's a trip home built into the promise. That's a lot to hear while lying on a rock.

The answer is False. The text says Jacob was afraid, and he says, “How awesome is this place!” (Gen 28:17) Just before that he says, “Surely the LORD is in this place, and I was unaware of it.” (Gen 28:16) That's the moment the fear shows up.

The answer is that he sets it up as a pillar and pours oil on it. “Early the next morning, Jacob took the stone that he had placed under his head, and he set it up as a pillar. He poured oil on top of it…” (Gen 28:18) The stone he slept on is now standing up. Same stone, new job. Right after that, he calls the place Bethel (Gen 28:19).

The answer is food to eat and clothes to wear. Jacob says, “…if He will provide me with food to eat and clothes to wear…” (Gen 28:20) It's one more IF in his vow. The next verse says he wants to return safely to his father's house (Gen 28:21). Food, clothes and a safe road home, friends.

The answer is tenth. Jacob says, “…of all that You give me I will surely give You a tenth.” (Gen 28:22) One out of every ten. Say a batch comes out of my oven with ten cookies. One of them goes to God. Notice he says “all” that God gives him, so nothing is left out of the count.
